assessment_summary: The statement claims that all unit-distance graphs in the Euclidean plane are 3-colorable. This is false, as shown by the classic Moser spindle construction. I provided explicit coordinates for the 7 vertices of the Moser spindle, verified that its 11 key edges have exactly unit length, and gave the standard proof that any attempt to 3-color these vertices leads to an immediate contradiction. Thus, the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane is at least 4.
counterexample:
Consider the Moser spindle, a graph with 7 vertices V = {A, B1, D1, C1, B2, D2, C2} placed at the following coordinates in the Euclidean plane:
A = (0, 0)
B1 = (√3/2, 1/2)
D1 = (√3/2, -1/2)
C1 = (√3, 0)
B2 = ((5√3 - √11)/12, (√33 + 5)/12)
D2 = ((5√3 + √11)/12, (√33 - 5)/12)
C2 = (5√3/6, √33/6)

This point set defines a unit-distance graph containing the following 11 edges of length exactly 1:
Diamond 1: {A,B1}, {A,D1}, {B1,D1}, {C1,B1}, {C1,D1}
Diamond 2: {A,B2}, {A,D2}, {B2,D2}, {C2,B2}, {C2,D2}
Connecting edge: {C1,C2}

(For instance, the distance squared between C1 and C2 is (5√3/6 - √3)^2 + (√33/6 - 0)^2 = (-√3/6)^2 + (√33/6)^2 = 3/36 + 33/36 = 36/36 = 1. Similar straightforward arithmetic confirms all 11 edges have length 1).

Suppose for contradiction that this graph is 3-colorable, meaning there is a proper vertex coloring c: V -> {1, 2, 3}.
In Diamond 1, A, B1, and D1 form a triangle, so their colors must be mutually distinct. Since C1 is adjacent to both B1 and D1, it must be assigned the only remaining color, which is the color of A. Thus, c(C1) = c(A).
By the exact same logic applied to Diamond 2, A, B2, and D2 form a triangle, so C2 must be assigned the color of A. Thus, c(C2) = c(A).
Consequently, c(C1) = c(C2). However, {C1,C2} is an edge, so they must have distinct colors in any valid proper coloring, yielding a contradiction.

Therefore, this graph is not 3-colorable, proving the statement invalid.
